533.title: Luqman's advice to his son
533.hook: Luqman the wise tells his son: don't associate anything with Allah (31:13)
533.howItsDone: Muslim parents and teachers often use Luqman's advice in 31:13–19 as a model for raising children, beginning with tawhid, the oneness of God.

segments.voice: Yesterday, tongues and colors, and your line was difference is a sign. Did you try the greeting, and how did it land? Day five hundred thirty-three, and a new surah.

Most of us can remember a piece of advice a parent gave us. Sometimes it was at a big moment, leaving home, a wedding, a hospital bed. Sometimes it was over the washing up, and we only realized years later that it had stuck. Surah Luqman, the thirty-first, is named for a man the Qur'an calls wise, and at its heart is a father talking to his son. It's the Qur'an's fullest speech of parenting advice, given line by line. Today, the first line.

Who was Luqman? The Qur'an says only that God gave him wisdom, hikma, and that the first thing wisdom meant was: give thanks to God. Beyond that, the sources are quiet. Later tradition says he was from Africa, perhaps Nubia or Abyssinia, and reports differ on whether he was a tailor, a carpenter or a shepherd. Most scholars say he was a wise man, not a prophet. The Qur'an doesn't settle it. What it does give is his words. Pickthall: "O my dear son! Ascribe no partners unto Allah. Lo! to ascribe partners (unto Him) is a tremendous wrong." Start with the first three words. In Arabic, ya bunayya. Not just my son, ibni, but the small, tender form, bunayya: my little son, my dear boy. The hardest, most important advice starts with affection. Then the content. Ascribing partners is shirk: treating anything else, money, power, a person, an idol, as if it shared God's place. And he calls it zulm 'azim, a tremendous wrong, an injustice. Zulm means putting something where it doesn't belong. There's a hadith in Bukhari that shows how much this verse mattered. When another verse said that safety belongs to those who don't mix their faith with zulm, the companions were frightened: which of us hasn't wronged himself? And the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ told them it doesn't mean that; it means what Luqman told his son, that shirk is a tremendous wrong. So the first advice is about putting first things first. Before manners, before prayer, before how to walk and talk, which come later in the speech: know who God is, and don't put anything in His place.
screen: `WHO WAS LUQMAN? THE QUR'AN IS QUIET.` · `YA BUNAYYA: MY DEAR SON.` · `SHIRK: A TREMENDOUS WRONG.` · `FIRST THINGS FIRST.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pass on one piece of good advice. Sit, and let the breath settle. Think of the best advice anyone ever gave you, the one that actually changed something. Who gave it? How did they say it? Was there tenderness in it? Now think of someone younger, or newer, who might need it: a child, a niece, a new colleague, a friend going through what you went through. Picture how you'd say it, starting the way Luqman did, with affection. If you pray, you can pray for that person by name. The bell holds the time.
Luqman's advice to his son. The wise man's speech in surah thirty-one, which starts, my dear son, and puts first: don't ascribe partners to God. Today's word.

534.title: Weakness upon weakness
534.hook: his mother carried him in weakness upon weakness, so thank Me and your parents (31:14)
534.howItsDone: Muslims treat kindness to parents, birr al-walidayn, as a major duty that follows directly after the worship of God, and many pray for their parents daily, living or dead.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Luqman's advice to his son, and your line was the first advice. Who did you pass your good advice to, and did you start kindly? Day five hundred thirty-four.

Ask anyone who has been pregnant about the last few weeks. The back that aches whatever you do. Sleeping propped on pillows. Getting up five times in the night. Then the birth itself. Then the newborn months, feeding through the night on almost no sleep, while the body is still recovering. In the middle of Luqman's advice to his son, the Qur'an suddenly interrupts, in God's own voice, to say something about exactly that.

Luqman has just told his son not to ascribe partners to God. And then, before his next piece of advice, there are two verses that aren't Luqman's. They're God speaking. We have enjoined on the human being concerning his parents. Pickthall: "His mother beareth him in weakness upon weakness, and his weaning is in two years". Then: give thanks to Me and to your parents; to Me is the journey's end. Weakness upon weakness, wahnan 'ala wahn. Commentators read it as weakness piled on weakness: the strain of pregnancy getting heavier month by month, then birth, then nursing. The verse sees it. Notice the order of the thanks. To Me, and to your parents. In one breath, gratitude to God and gratitude to the people who carried and raised you are joined. And then, the next verse adds a limit. If your parents strive to make you associate with God what you have no knowledge of, don't obey them. And yet, keep company with them in this world kindly. So even when you disagree with them about the most important thing, the kindness stays. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ underlined the mother's place. In a hadith in Bukhari and Muslim, a man asks who most deserves his good company. Your mother, the Prophet says. Then who? Your mother. Then who? Your mother. Then who? Your father. Many commentators connect the threefold mother to the three hardships in these verses: carrying, birth, nursing. Not every relationship with a mother is easy. The verse doesn't pretend it is. It just asks people to remember what was carried.
screen: `GOD'S VOICE INSIDE LUQMAN'S.` · `WAHNAN 'ALA WAHN.` · `THANK ME, AND YOUR PARENTS.` · `YOUR MOTHER, THREE TIMES.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: thank your mother, or pray for her. Sit, and let the breath settle. Think of your mother, or of whoever mothered you: a grandmother, an aunt, a foster parent, an older sister. Think of one specific thing she carried for you that you probably never thanked her for. A night shift. A school run. A meal she skipped. If she's alive and it's possible, decide how you'll thank her today. If she's gone, or if things are complicated, you can simply hold her in mind kindly. If you pray, you can pray for her. The bell holds the time.
Weakness upon weakness. The Qur'an's words for what a mother carries: pregnancy, birth and nursing, strain piled on strain. Today's word.

535.title: Walk modestly, lower your voice
535.hook: don't turn your cheek in scorn, walk modestly, lower your voice (31:18–19)
535.howItsDone: Muslims often teach Luqman's last pieces of advice, 31:17–19, as a short guide to manners: prayer, patience, humility, a moderate walk and a lowered voice.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the mother's burden, and your line was weakness upon weakness. Did you send the line of thanks, or say the prayer? Day five hundred thirty-five.

You can usually tell who thinks they're important before they say a word. The way they walk into a room, taking up the middle of the corridor. The way they half-turn their face away when someone they consider beneath them starts talking. The volume on the phone call in the train carriage. Luqman's advice to his son ends not with doctrine but with exactly this: how to hold your face, how to walk, and how loud to be.

Luqman has told his son to pray, to enjoin what's right, to forbid what's wrong, and to be patient with what befalls him. Then he gets physical. Pickthall: "Turn not thy cheek in scorn toward folk, nor walk with pertness in the land." The Arabic for turning the cheek is tusa''ir khaddak. Classical lexicons say the root sa'ar was a condition in camels that made them twist their necks to one side. So the picture is a person whose head is permanently turned away from others, as if they're not worth facing. And walking with pertness is marahan, strutting, walking in exultation. God doesn't love, the verse says, every arrogant boaster. Then the positive version. Pickthall: "Be modest in thy bearing and subdue thy voice." The first word is iqsid, from the same root as qasd, the middle, moderation. Not crawling and not strutting. A steady pace, aimed somewhere. And lower your voice, ughdud, the same verb used in the Qur'an for lowering the gaze. Then comes the line that makes children laugh when they first hear it: the harshest of all voices, the verse says, is the braying of the donkey. Loudness for its own sake isn't strength; it's just noise. This isn't a rule against ever raising your voice. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ called out to warn, and the call to prayer is meant to carry. It's about posture toward people: a face that turns toward them, a walk that doesn't take over the street, and a voice sized to the room.
screen: `TURN NOT THY CHEEK IN SCORN.` · `NO STRUTTING IN THE LAND.` · `IQSID: THE STEADY MIDDLE PACE.` · `LOWER YOUR VOICE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: speak softly today. Sit, and let the breath settle. Notice your face right now: is it turned toward anything, or away? Let it soften. Then think of the place where you're usually loudest: the kitchen, a meeting, the car, a group chat in capital letters. Picture the same moment with your voice brought down by half, your face turned toward the other person, your pace unhurried. Notice whether anything gets lost. If you pray, you can ask for a gentle voice. The bell holds the time.
Walk modestly. Luqman's advice on how to carry yourself: don't turn your cheek in scorn, don't strut, keep a steady pace, and lower your voice. Today's word.
Your line: lower your voice. Today, in the place you're usually loudest, try saying the same thing at half the volume. Day five hundred thirty-five.

536.title: If the sea were ink
536.hook: if every tree were pens and the sea ink, with seven more seas, His words would not run out (31:27)
536.howItsDone: Muslims often recite 31:27 and 18:109 when speaking of the vastness of God's knowledge and words, and calligraphers have written the verse many times.

segments.voice: Yesterday, walk modestly, and your line was lower your voice. Where were you usually loudest, and what happened at half the volume? Day five hundred thirty-six.

Before printing, writing was physical. A calligrapher cut a pen from a reed, sharpened it with a knife, dipped it, wrote a few words, dipped again. Ink was ground and mixed by hand, and it ran out. A copy of the Qur'an could take months. Every scribe knew the feeling of the pot running dry halfway through a line. Surah Luqman, near its end, takes that ordinary scribe's experience and stretches it until it breaks.
screen: `A REED PEN, A KNIFE, A POT OF INK.`

segments.voice: Pickthall: "And if all the trees in the earth were pens, and the sea, with seven more seas to help it, (were ink), the words of Allah could not be exhausted. Lo! Allah is Mighty, Wise." Try to picture it. Every tree on earth, every forest, every orchard, every palm, cut into pens. The aqlam, the reed pens. Then the ocean as the ink pot. Then seven more oceans poured in behind it. And the scribes write, and write, and the pens wear down, and the seas go dry, and the words of God are still not finished. Pickthall puts were ink in brackets because the Arabic leaves it out; the picture is so clear it doesn't need saying. The Qur'an has a shorter version of the same image in Surah Al-Kahf: if the sea were ink for the words of my Lord, the sea would run out before His words did, even if We brought another like it. What are the words? Commentators gave several answers. His knowledge, which has no edge. His commands, the be! by which everything comes into being. His wonders in creation, which no one could ever finish describing. Seven, in Arabic, often works as a number of abundance, not a precise count. The verse isn't measuring; it's overwhelming. And it makes something clear about every book, every sermon, every lesson, including this one. They're a few drops from that sea. Whatever has been said about God, there's always more. That isn't a frustration. For many Muslims it's a comfort: the source never runs dry.
screen: `EVERY TREE ON EARTH, A PEN.` · `THE SEA, AND SEVEN MORE, AS INK.` · `HIS KNOWLEDGE, COMMANDS AND WONDERS.` · `A FEW DROPS FROM THAT SEA.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: write one word of praise. Sit, and let the breath settle. Find a pen and a scrap of paper, or picture one. Think of one thing in the world that amazes you. The color of a sky. A child's laugh. The way a wound closes. Write one word for it, or one short line about God's work in it. Look at the word. Notice how much more there is that you didn't write. Let that feel like abundance, not failure. If you pray, you can say subhan Allah over it. The bell holds the time.
If the sea were ink. Luqman's picture of every tree as a pen and the sea, with seven more, as ink, and the words of God still not running out. Today's word.

segments.voice: Your line: the words don't run out. Today, keep the scrap with your word on it, and add one more word before you sleep. Day five hundred thirty-six.

537.title: Leaving their beds
537.hook: they forsake their beds to call on their Lord in fear and hope (32:16)
537.howItsDone: Many Muslims pray tahajjud, voluntary night prayer, in the last part of the night before the dawn prayer, especially in Ramadan, and many recite Surah As-Sajdah before sleeping.

segments.voice: Yesterday, if the sea were ink, and your line was the words don't run out. Did you add a second word to your scrap of paper before sleep? Day five hundred thirty-seven, and a new surah.

There's a particular quiet at about four in the morning. No traffic. No notifications. The fridge hums. A bird tries one note and stops. Shift workers know it, new parents know it, and so do people who get up on purpose, before dawn, to pray. Surah As-Sajdah, the Prostration, the thirty-second, is short, and it describes the believers in a single picture that has nothing to do with crowds or mosques. It's a picture of someone alone, at night, getting out of a warm bed.

The verse before describes those who, when reminded of God's signs, fall down in prostration; it's one of the places in the Qur'an where many Muslims prostrate as they recite, which is how the surah got its name. Then the picture. Pickthall: "Who forsake their beds to cry unto their Lord in fear and hope". The Arabic is vivid: tatajafa junubuhum 'an al-madaji', their sides draw away from their beds. As if the body itself pulls back from sleep. And notice the two words: fear and hope, khawfan wa tama'an. Not one or the other. The night prayer holds both, the honesty about what's wrong and the reaching toward mercy. The practice is called qiyam al-layl, standing in the night. Another name is tahajjud, from a root that means waking from sleep. A hadith in Tirmidhi says the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, explaining to Mu'adh ibn Jabal the doors of good, mentioned a person's prayer in the middle of the night, and then recited this very verse. And a hadith in Bukhari and Muslim says that in the last third of every night, God descends to the nearest heaven and asks: who is calling on Me, that I may answer him? Who is asking of Me, that I may give him? It's voluntary, not one of the five prayers. Many people do it only sometimes, a few short units, two or four or more, in the dark. The Prophet, it's reported, recited this surah before sleeping. So the verse is about the cost: a warm bed, a little sleep. And what's bought with it is a conversation nobody else hears.
screen: `THEIR SIDES DRAW AWAY FROM THEIR BEDS.` · `IN FEAR AND IN HOPE.` · `QIYAM AL-LAYL, TAHAJJUD.` · `THE LAST THIRD OF THE NIGHT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: wake briefly before dawn. Sit, and let the breath settle. Picture tonight. If it's safe and sensible for your sleep, decide to set an alarm a little before dawn, even fifteen minutes before you'd normally rise. Picture the quiet, the dark room, the cold floor. Picture sitting up and doing one small thing with that time: if you pray, two short units of prayer, or a few words of your own; if you don't, a few minutes of stillness and gratitude. Then back to sleep, or into the day. The bell holds the time.
Qiyam al-layl. Standing in the night: the voluntary prayer of people whose sides draw away from their beds, in fear and hope. Today's word.
Your line: up in the night. Tonight, set the alarm you pictured, and put it where you'll have to sit up to reach it. Day five hundred thirty-seven.

538.title: Hidden joy
538.hook: no soul knows what joy is kept hidden for them (32:17)
538.howItsDone: Many Muslims value hidden good deeds, such as secret charity and night prayer, and recite 32:17 alongside the hadith of what no eye has seen when speaking of paradise.

segments.voice: Yesterday, qiyam al-layl, and your line was up in the night. Did the alarm go off, and what did you do with the quiet? Day five hundred thirty-eight.

The best gifts are the ones you can't guess. A box handed over with a grin, and someone saying, don't shake it. Half the joy is not knowing. The other half is realizing, when you open it, that the giver knew you better than you thought. As-Sajdah has just described people getting out of bed in the dark to pray, unseen. And the very next verse says what's waiting for them. Or rather, it says something more interesting: that nobody knows.

Pickthall: "No soul knoweth what is kept hid for them of joy, as a reward for what they used to do." The phrase Pickthall translates joy is qurrat a'yun, literally, coolness of the eyes. It's an old Arabic idiom. In a hot land, coolness is relief; and many explain that tears of grief are hot, while tears of happiness are cool. So qurrat 'ayn is the thing that cools your eyes, that makes you deeply, quietly glad. The same phrase is used elsewhere in the Qur'an for a child, a spouse, the baby Musa returned to his mother. Here, it's kept hidden. Ukhfiya, concealed. A hadith in Bukhari brings this verse to life. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ said that God says: I have prepared for My righteous servants what no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and has never occurred to any human heart. And Abu Hurayra, who reported it, added: recite if you wish, no soul knows what is kept hidden for them. Some early commentators noticed a symmetry. The people in the verse before prayed in secret, at night, where no one could see. So their reward is secret too. A hidden deed, answered with a hidden joy. It's a kind of justice, and a kind of tenderness. The Qur'an gives many pictures of paradise: gardens, rivers, shade, fruit. This verse quietly says that all the pictures fall short. Whatever you imagine, it isn't that. It's more. And that leaves room for hope that doesn't need to be described to be real.

Pay for someone's coffee and leave before they notice. Leave an anonymous kind note. Fix something broken at home before anyone sees it's broken. Give to a cause and tell no one. Picture doing it, and picture keeping it to yourself afterward, even when you're tempted to mention it. If you pray, you can offer it quietly. The bell holds the time.

539.title: A beautiful example
539.hook: in the messenger of Allah you have a beautiful example (33:21)
539.howItsDone: Muslims follow the sunnah, the Prophet's example, in worship and in daily habits, learning it from the hadith collections and from biographies of his life.

segments.voice: Yesterday, hidden joy, and your line was joy kept hidden. Did you manage to keep your secret good a secret? Day five hundred thirty-nine, the end of the week, and a new surah.

Medina, the year 627, winter. An army of ten thousand, a confederacy of tribes, is marching on the city. On the advice of Salman the Persian, the Muslims decide to do something unheard of in Arabia: dig a trench across the open northern side of the city. Thousands of men with picks and baskets, in the cold, short on food, racing against time. And among them, carrying earth on his back until the dust covered his skin, the leader of the community. Surah Al-Ahzab, the Confederates, the thirty-third, tells of those days.

The surah describes the fear honestly. Eyes grew wild, hearts reached the throats, and people began to think all kinds of thoughts about God. Some slipped away with excuses. And right in the middle of that account comes the verse. Pickthall: "Verily in the messenger of Allah ye have a good example for him who looketh unto Allah and the Last Day, and remembereth Allah much." The Arabic is uswatun hasanah. Hasanah is good, beautiful, excellent. Uswah is a model, a pattern, someone you copy. And the context matters. The verse isn't on a poster. It's in a trench. What did the example look like there? Bukhari reports that the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ dug and carried earth alongside everyone, chanting verses with them as they worked. Jabir reported that when a huge rock blocked the digging, the Prophet came and broke it, and that he had a stone tied against his stomach from hunger, the same as the rest. The example wasn't in how he talked about hardship. It was in how he did the hardship with them. That's what Muslims mean by following the sunnah, the Prophet's way. Not only the prayers and fasts, but the small things: smiling, which a hadith calls charity; helping at home, which 'A'isha said he did, mending and serving his family; greeting first; eating with the right hand. The Qur'an uses uswah of Ibrahim, too. This week was full of people worth copying: Luqman's first advice, a mother's weakness upon weakness, a lowered voice, words that don't run out, up in the night, joy kept hidden. And today: a beautiful example.

Picture exactly when in your day you'll do it. If you're not Muslim, you can still pick one as a kindness worth trying. If you pray, you can send blessings on him. The bell holds the time.
